title: Password Policy Discovery
summary: Password policy discovery is the collection of the rules that govern credentials in a network or cloud environment: minimum length, character complexity, history depth, maximum age and account lockout thresholds. The policy itself is not secret and is readable by ordinary authenticated users, which is exactly why it is useful to an intruder preparing a brute force or password spraying attempt. Knowing the minimum length tells the attacker which guesses are wasted; knowing the lockout threshold tells them how many attempts they can make per account before the account is disabled, which is the difference between a quiet campaign and a wave of locked-out users. Windows exposes this through the net accounts command and through directory service cmdlets, Unix-like systems through tools such as chage and the pluggable authentication module configuration, macOS through policy tools, network devices through their own command line interfaces, and cloud providers through policy read interfaces. Detection is not about a single command, because administrators run the same queries during audit work; it is about who runs them, how often, and whether the query is followed by authentication failures.

beginner.definition: Every network has rules about passwords, for example how long they must be. This technique is an attacker looking up those rules. They do it before trying to guess passwords. The rules tell them how to guess without being locked out.
beginner.whyItMatters: If an attacker knows your lockout limit is five tries, they will stop at four. That keeps the attack quiet, because no account gets locked. They also learn which password guesses are worth trying, such as twelve character phrases instead of short words. Your policy then becomes a guide that helps them, unless you also watch for the lookups.
howItWorks: The attacker already has some access, often a normal user account on the network.
They run a command or interface call that reports the password rules in force.
On Windows they use the net accounts command or directory service policy cmdlets.
On Linux or macOS they read the password aging settings or the authentication configuration files.
On network devices they use the device command line to show authentication policy settings.
In cloud accounts they call the policy read interface and then plan guesses that fit the rules.
beginner.example: Think of a post office with a sign saying staff may try three times at the code lock before it freezes. A thief reads the sign and tries exactly twice on each lock in the building. Nothing ever freezes, no alarm sounds, and the mail keeps moving. The sign was there to help staff, but it also told the thief how far to push.
takeaways: Longer minimum lengths and lockout limits both reduce the value of a guessing campaign.
Treat repeated policy queries as reconnaissance, especially from service or helpdesk accounts.
Alert on many failed logins across many accounts, which is spraying spread thinly.

objectives: Explain what a password policy contains and why an attacker wants to read it.
Identify where password policy settings live on Windows, Linux, macOS and cloud platforms.
Recall that Windows exposes policy through the net accounts command and directory service cmdlets.
Describe how lockout thresholds and minimum length shape the choices in a guessing attack.
Name the log sources that show policy discovery and the follow-on authentication failures.
